title: A Weathervane, Not a Map — Adrian Wedd
note: Fresh notebook created for this post (458 notebooks on the account, so no reuse pressure). Source restricted to the essay itself via --source-ids so the artifacts cannot drift into other material.

audio.focus: Create a long, substantive deep dive into Adrian Wedd's essay 'A Weathervane, Not a Map'. This is field notes from working with AI agents, structured as a weather report rather than a methodology. Open with the concrete frame: the essayist hates how-to-use-AI advice and reads papers and vendor manuals instead. Then walk the receipts in order. (1) The semantic-verification machinery that flagged an alarming claim that 85 per cent of children with ADHD experience a dopamine crash when stimulant medication wears off — a claim absent from every committed edition of the manuscript, cited to a line number that is a bullet about collaborative problem solving and that reappears against three different chapters in three different review reports. Preserve the essay's honest conclusion that the committed record cannot distinguish a finding about a version that never entered the repository from a reviewer constructing a claim out of the section it was reading. (2) The Bottom Pub property monitor that faithfully answered a narrower question than the humans thought they had asked, and reported unchanged while the pub was listed for sale elsewhere. (3) SPARK, where a docstring on a method inside GpioLeaseGuard changed the Python abstract syntax tree and three daemons were restarted for prose. (4) Undertow accumulating 131 lanes, 48 of them registered worktrees, and 15.5 GiB of sibling checkouts until isolation became an estate, and the resulting principle that a registry entry is a claim about a process, not evidence of one. (5) Scaffolding's half-life, and Anthropic's and OpenAI's current manuals telling developers to revisit assumptions encoded for earlier models, including instructions buried in skills and AGENTS.md files. Distinguish throughout between observed incidents, derived and inferred conclusions, and the essay's own explicit forecast that its interpretation will partly expire. Note the four working beliefs: reality outranks representation, verification should target the property you actually care about, failure is worth preserving, and consequence matters more than complexity. Close on 'delegation should compress concern', and on the weathervane giving reality another vote. Thoughtful, technically literate discussion with dry Australian humour. Attribute the essay to Adrian Wedd. No invented evidence, no fabricated numbers, no claims of machine consciousness.

Slow deliberate pacing, long holds, no rapid cutting. Adapt 'A Weathervane, Not a Map' by Adrian Wedd. Preserve observed facts versus derived and inferred conclusions: the 85 per cent ADHD dopamine-crash claim absent from every committed edition, the Bottom Pub monitor answering a narrower question than the humans asked, three daemons restarted because a docstring changed an abstract syntax tree, 131 lanes and 48 registered worktrees and 15.5 GiB of checkouts, and the vendors' own manuals recommending that assumptions encoded for earlier models be revisited.
